name: Icon button
summary: Triggers an action with an icon alone; its label is given to assistive technology.
description: An icon button performs an action, like a button, but shows only an icon: it saves room in toolbars, table rows and headers where the action is familiar enough to be recognized from its symbol. It has no visible text, so it always carries a label that assistive technology announces as its name. Like every button, it never navigates.

anatomy.description: Interactive, square root. Receives focus, carries background, border, size, the state styling and the accessible name.
Glyph of the icon font, the only visible content. Takes the color a label would take. Hidden from assistive technology: the container's name says what it means.

properties.name: Emphasis
properties.description: Visual weight of the icon button, from strongest to weakest.

options.description: Highest emphasis: strong fill in the intent color, contrasting glyph.
Medium emphasis: tinted fill and light border in the intent color. The default.
Lowest emphasis: glyph only at rest; a tinted fill and a light border appear on hover and press.

properties.name: Intent
properties.description: Kind of action, independent of emphasis. Every intent exists at every emphasis.

options.description: Generic actions that carry no brand or status meaning.
Actions that carry the brand color: the main path through a flow.
Destructive or irreversible actions (delete, remove, revoke).

properties.name: Size
properties.description: Square side (minimum width and height), padding, corner radius and glyph size scale together: at the default text size the side is the height of the button of the same size, the glyph the size of its icon.

options.description: Very dense UIs: inline in table cells, compact lists. Exactly the 24 x 24 px minimum target on the web.
Marketing surfaces, primary call to action on a page.

properties.name: Icon
properties.description: Material Symbols name of the glyph (add, delete, more_vert). Choose a symbol people already associate with the action.

properties.name: Label
properties.description: Accessible name of the button, never drawn in it and shown as a tooltip where people hover or focus: names the action, not the symbol (Delete row, not Trash).

properties.name: Disabled
properties.description: Prevents activation; hover and active feedback no longer apply. Prefer keeping actions enabled and validating on activation.

states.description: Pointer over the container. Needs a pointing device: touch has no hover. Fill and border move one step along the intent ramp; the glyph keeps its color, except a ghost brand glyph, which takes the tinted fill's brand color.
Pointer, finger or key pressed down: the press state. Fill and border move a second step along the intent ramp.
Keyboard focus. Shows the shared focus ring outside the border; pointer focus shows none.
Non-interactive. Colors drop to the shared disabled palette whatever the emphasis and intent; hover and active do not apply.

notes: The container is a square: minimum width and minimum height both come from the size option, so the container stays square at every size. At the default text size its side is the height of the button of the same size.

The padding is a minimum on every side, the button's block padding: at the default text size the minimum side sets the size and the glyph sits centered in the square; when the glyph grows with the text size and outgrows it, the square grows to the glyph plus the padding, as high as a button of the same size with an icon.
The glyph box is the icon size of the size option, the size of the button's icon, at the default text size; it grows with the text size (Iconography rule text-size).

name.text: Computed from the label property, which the container carries as its accessible label (aria-label on the web). The glyph is hidden from assistive technology and adds nothing to the name.

keyboard.action: Moves focus to the button. A disabled button is not focusable and is skipped.

guidelines.text: Expose the button role, its name and its disabled state through the platform's native button control rather than a custom view, so assistive technology receives them without extra work.
Use the native button element: it exposes the role and the disabled state without ARIA. Do not add role="button" to it.

The icon button can be reached and activated from a keyboard, physical or assistive, on every platform. The platform provides this to its native button control through its own keyboard services, so the control needs no keyboard handling of its own; the keys are the platform's.

Use the native button so Full Keyboard Access can reach and activate it, and test the app with Full Keyboard Access on. On iPadOS, do not add keyboard navigation of your own to the button: Full Keyboard Access activates controls.
With a hardware keyboard or Switch Access, focus navigation reaches the icon button and highlights it, in a logical order, and focus can always move away from it.
On macOS, Full Keyboard Access lets people navigate to the icon button and activate it with the keyboard alone: use the native control and keep the standard keyboard shortcuts.
Use an icon button for actions and a link for navigation: the role must match the function the control provides.
Every icon button has a name that describes its purpose: the label property is required, because the icon is the only visible content and a control made of non-text content needs a name.
The label is set as aria-label on the button, which takes precedence over its content in the accessible name computation.
Hide the glyph with aria-hidden="true": an icon-font glyph is written as its ligature name (delete, more_vert), which would otherwise be read.
Give the button an alternative label for VoiceOver: the icon alone does not describe the action.
Pass the label as the contentDescription of the icon inside the IconButton: the framework cannot describe a graphic element on its own.
With no visible text, WCAG 2.5.3 Label in Name does not apply; the name describes the function, not the symbol.

Show the label in a tooltip when the pointer rests on the icon button and when it receives keyboard focus, so people who do not recognize the symbol can read the action. The tooltip can be dismissed with Escape without moving the pointer or focus, stays while the pointer moves over it, and stays until hover or focus leaves. The reference implementation draws none until the system has a Tooltip component.
Never show the label with the title attribute: browsers show it on pointer hover only, never on keyboard focus or touch.
On macOS the system displays a tooltip after people hover over a button for a moment: give the icon button one, a brief phrase that says what it does, like its label.

iPhone and iPad apps that run on a Mac show tooltips when the pointer rests on an element: give the icon button one there too. On touch there is no hover and no tooltip, so the symbol alone carries the action; when a short text says it more clearly, use a button with a label.
Never rely on color alone to convey emphasis or intent: an error-intent icon button names the consequence in its label and uses a symbol that shows it.

The glyph is non-text content (a symbol), so it needs 3:1 against the container background in every color mode, emphasis, intent and enabled state; it takes the icon colors of the mapped roles, which equal the button's label colors (decision same-rendering-as-button). They clear 3:1 everywhere and, since the Figma library's POC2 export, the 4.5:1 of text too (lowest 4.56:1, accent error at rest). Disabled icon buttons are inactive and exempt.
The glyph, not the border, identifies the control: the light borders of the subtle and ghost emphases, and the absent border of a ghost icon button at rest, need no 3:1 boundary contrast.
A visible focus indicator appears when the icon button receives keyboard focus, and contrasts at least 3:1 with the adjacent colors in every color mode.

The focus ring is 2.4 px thick and drawn outside the border, so it covers at least the area of a 2 CSS pixel thick perimeter of the button at 3:1 or more, as WCAG 2.4.13 Focus Appearance asks (AAA, adopted as extra quality).
The focus ring is drawn with :focus-visible, so pointer focus shows no ring.
Every size is a pointer target of at least 24 x 24 CSS pixels: the container is a square whose side is the minimum height; extra small sits exactly at that minimum.

Every size has a hit region of at least 44 x 44 pt, as Apple recommends: the extra small, small and medium squares (24, 28 and 36 pt) keep their drawn size and the hit region extends around them, centered, with the layout reserving it so that the hit regions of neighbouring controls do not overlap.

Every size has a touch target of at least 48 x 48 dp, as Android recommends: the square (24, 28, 36 or 44 dp) keeps its drawn size and is centered in 48 dp of reserved layout space, with the touch target extended to it (Compose: the minimumInteractiveComponentSize modifier, which Material's IconButton already applies).

Text can be resized up to 200 percent; the criterion covers text, not icons, which are non-text content. The glyph grows with the text all the same, as every icon that carries meaning on its own does: people who need larger text also need to read the symbol that names the action. The square grows with it and keeps the padding around the glyph, so it stays as high as a button of the same size with an icon.

Text sizes are px lengths today, which a browser's text-only size setting does not change: that setting enlarges neither the button labels nor the glyph, while zoom enlarges both, which meets Resize Text. When text follows that setting, the glyph follows it with it.
The glyph grows with Dynamic Type, up to the larger accessibility sizes, as Apple asks of meaningful interface icons; the square grows with it.
macOS does not support Dynamic Type: on macOS, the icon button keeps its size, as text does.

The native disabled attribute removes the button from the focus order. When people need to discover why an action is unavailable, keep the button enabled and explain on activation, or keep it focusable with aria-disabled.
Always include a press state: without one a custom button feels unresponsive. The active state is that press state.
Color transitions are removed when the user asks for reduced motion.
The transition is switched off under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce.
When the Reduce Motion setting is on, reduce automatic and repetitive animations.

guidelines: The label names the action, starting with a verb: Delete row, Close dialog, More actions. Never the name of the symbol (Trash, X, Dots).
Keep labels short: one to three words, like a button label.
Use an icon button only when the symbol is familiar for the action; otherwise use a button with a text label.
With the error intent, the label names the consequence: Delete project, Remove member.

examples.name: Ghost neutral
examples.description: Overflow menu of a card or a row.

examples.name: Ghost error, small
examples.description: Destructive action repeated in a list: the label names what is deleted.

decisions.text: Without an emphasis, an icon button is subtle, like the button (Button decision default-emphasis-subtle). An explicit emphasis renders as before. The icon=only variant of the Figma prototype's Button set defaults to accent.
decisions.rationale: A button or icon button left at its default should neither outweigh the content it sits in nor lose the look of a button: subtle lowers the emphasis so that accent is no longer what every button gets by omission, and its tinted fill and light border keep the visible shape of a button, which ghost only shows on hover and press. Accent is chosen on purpose, for the one action that must stand out; ghost for actions repeated among content.

decisions.text: The icon button has no pressed (on or off) state: it triggers an action and its look never says that something stays on. An action that stays on or off (favorite, mute, bold) is a toggle button, a component of its own that the system does not have yet; until then, a setting turned on or off in a list or a form is a switch.
decisions.rationale: A toggle button needs its own decisions: its look when on for every emphasis and intent, with no selected role in the semantic tier, its states while on, its groups. Each platform treats it as a toggle with its own state (aria-pressed on the web, a button that behaves like a toggle with a background that shows its state on Apple platforms, toggleable with a state description on Android), which a component of its own carries, as the framework themes' toggles do.

decisions.text: The icon button grows with the text size on every platform that lets people raise it, as a button of the same size with an icon does (Iconography decision icons-follow-text-size): the glyph grows with the text, and the square keeps its side as a minimum and a minimum padding on every side, the button's block padding (space.2 / 3 / 5 / 8, extra small to large). At the default text size nothing moves; when the glyph outgrows the square, the square grows to the glyph plus that padding and stays as high as the button next to it. Where nothing scales the text (macOS) and on the web, where text and glyph are px lengths that zoom scales together, the icon button keeps its size.
decisions.rationale: The glyph is an icon that carries meaning on its own, which the Iconography foundation and Apple ask to grow with the text. Growing like the button keeps an icon button and a button of the same size lined up at every text size, as the mirror wants; growing in proportion would make it taller than the button next to it, and keeping it fixed would leave the symbol at its default size next to text two or three times larger.

decisions.text: On iOS and Android every size reaches the platform's touch target without growing: the hit region is at least 44 x 44 pt on iOS and 48 x 48 dp on Android, centered on the drawn square, and the layout reserves it so that neighbouring targets do not overlap (on Android the minimumInteractiveComponentSize modifier, as Material's IconButton does). The drawn square, the glyph and the tokens stay the same on every platform, as in Figma and on the Button it mirrors. The web (WCAG 2.5.8, 24 x 24 CSS px) and desktop already meet their targets and keep the drawn square as the target.
decisions.rationale: The extra small to medium squares were under Apple's 44 pt and every size under Android's 48 dp, and icon buttons are the smallest controls of the system, often set in rows. Both platforms let a control keep a smaller drawn size with a larger touch area around it, which keeps one rendering everywhere instead of platform sizes.

decisions.text: Wherever people hover with a pointer or move keyboard focus, the label is also shown on screen as a tooltip, on hover and on keyboard focus alike. On the web the tooltip meets WCAG 1.4.13 (dismissible with Escape, hoverable, persistent) and follows the APG Tooltip pattern, never the title attribute; on macOS, and for iPhone and iPad apps running on a Mac, it is the system tooltip. On touch there is no hover: the symbol alone carries the action, or a button with a text label replaces the icon button. Android says nothing: no trusted Android source covers tooltips. The tooltip itself, and how it relates to the accessible name (a description repeating the label, or the tooltip naming the button), belong to a Tooltip component the system does not have yet; the reference implementation draws none until then.
decisions.rationale: The label is the only statement of the action and was never shown: sighted people who do not recognize the symbol had nothing to read, while the platforms with hover already show a button's name this way.

decisions.text: Being reached and activated from a keyboard is a requirement on every platform (WCAG 2.1.1 on the web, EN 301 549 11.2.1.1.1 for native software), met through the native button control and the platform's own keyboard services; only the keys are per platform. The web keeps its keys (Tab, Enter, Space, from APG). iOS and macOS rely on Full Keyboard Access, with no custom keyboard navigation for the button on iPadOS; Android relies on focus navigation, reached and highlighted in a logical order. No key is named for iOS, Android or desktop: no trusted source of those platforms names them.
decisions.rationale: The keyboard requirement holds everywhere; the contract said it for the web only.

decisions.text: The glyph keeps the roles of the Button's label decisions rather than the role of the fill it sits on: subtle neutral, and ghost neutral in every state, read global.icon.on-base.neutral.primary although the subtle fill has its own role (global.icon.on-subtle.neutral.default), as in button decision neutral-label-primary; ghost error reads global.icon.on-subtle.functional.error.default in every state, at rest with no fill too, as in button decision error-label-figma-library. The Icon button renders the same as the Button (same-rendering-as-button), so these roles change only with the Button's decisions.
decisions.rationale: The Button already decided these colors; the icon button renders the same as the button in the end.

decisions.text: Without a size, an icon button is medium (36 px), like the button (Button decision default-size-medium). The icon=only variant of the Figma prototype's Button set defaults to xsmall.
decisions.rationale: Every component with sizes in the system defaults to medium (text field, select, search field, number field, textarea, dropdown, icon button), so controls placed together without a size get the same size step; the prototype's xsmall default is also the top-left variant of its Button set and may come from the set's layout rather than from a choice.

decisions.text: The icon button always renders the same as the button of the same emphasis, intent, size and state, as the icon=only variant of the Button in the Figma prototype does: its square side is the button's height, its glyph is the button's icon (size, font and optical size), and its fills, borders and glyph colors are the button's fills, borders and label colors, through the icon role of the same name (global.icon.* aliases global.text.*). Corners, border width, focus ring and transitions are the button's too. A button decision on any of these applies to the icon button in the same change: pnpm validate fails when an icon button token differs from the button token at the same place.

The square side is the button's height, space.24 / 28 / 36 / 44 from extra small to large, with the same 24 px floor at extra small so that every size meets WCAG 2.2 2.5.8 by its own size; the Figma prototype's icon=only square is 20 px at extra small. The glyph is the button's icon, size.2 / 3 / 4 / 4 (16 / 20 / 24 / 24 px), as in Figma, in Material Symbols Outlined (font.icon.*: fill off, weight 300, grade 0, optical size 20 at every size). The glyph sits centered in the square: Figma's padding (2 / 4 / 6 / 10 px) is the side minus the glyph, halved, and needs no token. Corners corner-radius.2xs / 2xs / xs / xs, border stroke-width.sm, transitions duration.fast and easing.standard, as before.

The icon button takes the button's color decisions of 0.19.0 and 0.20.0. Subtle and ghost neutral glyphs are global.icon.on-base.neutral.primary in every state and both modes (button decision neutral-label-primary); a ghost brand glyph at rest is global.icon.on-base.brand.default (ghost-brand-label-on-base); a ghost icon button takes the subtle border one step behind on hover and press, global.border.subtle.<family>.default / hover (ghost-border-one-step-behind), and the shared disabled fill and border when disabled (ghost-disabled-shared). Error glyphs keep the Figma library's error colors (error-label-figma-library).

The icon button exists in every color mode of the system, light and dark, and takes the colors of the mode of its context. Every color aliases the Figma library's mapped roles as they are, in both modes: fills global.bg.<emphasis>.<family>.<state>, borders global.border.<emphasis>.<family>.<state>, glyph global.icon.on-<emphasis>.<family>, disabled global.*.state.disabled.default; a ghost icon button reads the subtle text and icon colors. Where the Figma library's error colors fall under WCAG 2.2 AA, the gap is kept and tracked, not corrected in the icon button.
decisions.rationale: The Figma library as it is, errors and limitations included, is the starting point the system evolves from.

decisions.text: Sizes, spacing, radii, borders, type, icons and motion come straight from the Figma library's scales and the design system's additions, with the same values as before and no semantic layer in between: icons are Material Symbols Outlined glyphs (font.icon.*: fill off, weight 300, grade 0, optical size 20) at size.2 / 2 / 3 / 4, extra small to large; minimum width and height space.24 / 32 / 40 / 48; corners corner-radius.2xs / 2xs / xs / xs; border stroke-width.sm; transitions duration.fast and easing.standard.

The icon button exists in every color mode of the system, light and dark, and takes the colors of the mode of its context. Its color decisions (emphasis, intent, state) are the same in every mode; only the semantic colors they alias change. Dark colors follow the prototype's dark mapping, with the error fill and border kept one step darker than the prototype, as in light mode.
Every icon button has a required label that is its accessible name, given to the button itself (aria-label on the web); the glyph is hidden from assistive technology.
Icons are glyphs of Material Symbols, latest version, for every component: Outlined family with fill off, weight 300, grade 0 and optical size 20 px.

changelog.note: Fix, no decision changed: the label property no longer says the label is never shown (decision name-shown-as-tooltip shows it as a tooltip). Docs: the iOS and Android paragraphs of Sizes no longer repeat the Accessibility section, the glyph takes the icon color that matches the button's label (decision glyph-roles-from-button), and Content no longer says most people never see the label. No token, CSS, template or rendering change.

Decision default-emphasis-subtle: an icon button without an emphasis is subtle instead of accent, as the button. Template default and docs updated; an explicit emphasis renders as before. Departs from the Figma prototype, whose icon=only variant defaults to accent. No token or CSS change; contrast unchanged.

Decision no-pressed-state: the icon button has no pressed state; actions that stay on or off wait for a Toggle button component, and a setting in a list or a form is a switch. The docs no longer send toggling actions to a toggle button the system does not have. Three references added (Apple HIG Toggles, Android accessibility principles). No token, CSS, template or rendering change.

Decision grows-with-text-size: the glyph grows with the text size on every platform that scales text, and the square grows with it as a button with an icon does, keeping a minimum padding on every side. New component tokens icon-button.container.padding.* (space.2 / 3 / 5 / 8, the button's block padding, mirrored); layout sizing hug instead of fixed. New guidelines for every platform (WCAG 1.4.4), the web, iOS and macOS, five references. At the default text size nothing moves: same sizes on every platform, contrast unchanged.

Decision touch-target-hit-region: on iOS every size has a hit region of at least 44 x 44 pt and on Android a touch target of at least 48 x 48 dp, centered on the drawn square and reserved in the layout; the drawn square is unchanged. The iOS and Android guidelines no longer say the sizes fall under the platform targets. No token, CSS, template or rendering change; contrast unchanged.

Decision name-shown-as-tooltip: where people hover or move keyboard focus, the label is also shown as a tooltip (web: WCAG 1.4.13 and the APG Tooltip pattern, never title; macOS and iPhone or iPad apps on a Mac: the system tooltip); on touch the symbol carries the action. New web, desktop and iOS guidelines and five references. The reference implementation draws no tooltip until the system has a Tooltip component. No token or rendering change.

Decision keyboard-on-every-platform: the icon button is reached and activated from a keyboard on every platform (WCAG 2.1.1, EN 301 549 11.2.1.1.1), through the native control and the platform's keyboard services; new guidelines for iOS (Full Keyboard Access), Android (focus navigation) and desktop (macOS Full Keyboard Access). The web keys are unchanged. No token or rendering change.

Decision glyph-roles-from-button: subtle and ghost neutral glyphs keep global.icon.on-base.neutral.primary, and ghost error glyphs global.icon.on-subtle.functional.error.default, as the Button's label does (neutral-label-primary, error-label-figma-library), rather than the role of the fill they sit on. No token change, so contrast is unchanged: lowest glyph contrast on the page and on a card, light 16.01:1 (subtle neutral, active) and 6.30:1 (ghost error, active), dark 5.55:1 (subtle neutral, active) and 8.49:1 (ghost error).

Follows the Iconography foundation 0.5.0 (decision glyphs-follow-reading-direction): in a right-to-left layout, a directional glyph flips horizontally, like the Button's icons (same-rendering-as-button). Web: the template marks it with data-directional, flipped under :dir(rtl). No token change.

Follows Button decision icon-optical-size-24 (same-rendering-as-button) and the Iconography foundation 0.3.0: the glyph is drawn for optical size 24 instead of 20 (icon-button.icon.optical-size → font.icon.optical-size.24). sizes-from-button restated optical size 20; that value is now 24. Sizes and colors unchanged, so contrast is unchanged.

Fix, no decision changed: the Figma library's POC2 export (Color foundation 3.1.0) moves the values of the roles the tokens alias; the tokens, CSS and template are unchanged. Light: 25 tokens follow the ash retune (one to four units per channel); container.background.accent.error.default reads global.bg.accent.functional.error.default: #E12A23 becomes #DF2821; icon.color.* (6 tokens) reads global.icon.on-subtle.functional.error.default: #C01619 becomes #940E11. Dark: 14 tokens follow the ash retune (one to four units per channel); container.background.accent.error.default reads global.bg.accent.functional.error.default: #E12A23 becomes #DF2821; container.border-color.accent.neutral.default reads global.border.accent.neutral.default: #B9B7B7 becomes #CFCFCF; icon.color.ghost.brand.default reads global.icon.on-base.brand.default: #9EE7FA becomes #41B9D3.

Fix: the focus ring shows on keyboard focus, as Button 0.22.1. The ring rule was wrapped in :where(), so the :focus reset (outline: none) outranked it; it now uses :is() and wins by source order. No token or decision changes.
Decision default-size-medium: an icon button without a size stays medium, like the button (Button 0.22.0), rather than the Figma prototype's xsmall default. No token or rendering change.

Decisions same-rendering-as-button, sizes-from-button (supersedes figma-library-scales) and colors-from-button: the icon button renders like the button since Button 0.21.0, as the Figma prototype's icon=only variant of the Button does. Square side 24 / 28 / 36 / 44 px (was 24 / 32 / 40 / 48), glyph 16 / 20 / 24 / 24 px (was 16 / 16 / 20 / 24): an icon button now lines up with a button of the same size. Subtle and ghost neutral glyphs are the primary text color, a ghost brand glyph at rest the surface brand color, a ghost icon button gains the subtle border one step behind on hover and press and the shared disabled fill and border. Glyph contrast over the level 0 and level 1 surfaces, every emphasis x intent x enabled state: light 3.29:1 or more (subtle error, pressed; neutral glyphs 15.99:1 or more, were 10.80), dark 4.48:1 or more (accent error, rest; neutral glyphs 5.55:1 or more, were 6.46); 3:1 required (WCAG 1.4.11). The error intent still misses 4.5:1 in places. Focus ring unchanged. iOS: the large icon button reaches 44 pt; Android: every size is under 48 dp. CSS and template unchanged.

Decisions figma-library-colors and figma-library-scales: the tokens are recreated from the Figma library (Color foundation 3.0.0). Component tokens keep their paths and the CSS is unchanged; the glyph now aliases the Figma library's icon roles (global.icon.on-<emphasis>.<family>, the same values as the text roles) and fills and borders its global.bg / global.border roles. Visible changes: the error colors follow the Figma library (accent error fill error 500 / 600 / 700, border 600 / 700 / 800, glyph on tinted error fills error 600), and dark mode is the Figma library's dark mapping. Glyph contrast over the level 0 and level 1 surfaces, every platform: light 3.28:1 or more, dark 4.46:1 or more (3:1 required, WCAG 1.4.11); the error intent no longer reaches 4.5:1 everywhere. Focus ring light 5.46:1 or more, dark 9.61:1 or more. Sizes, radii, border, icons and motion alias the Figma library's scales and the icon font and motion additions directly instead of the repository's invented semantic tokens: same values, no visual change. iOS and Android lose the overlays that raised the extra small, small and medium sizes to 44 pt and 48 dp.

Decision color-modes. The system gains a dark mode (tokens/modes/dark/, the prototype's Colors / Mapped dark) next to the default light mode. Component tokens, CSS and template unchanged: the icon button reads the same variables, which resolve again in every data-theme context (light, dark, auto) on the web and in the per-mode trees of the other platforms. Dark contrast, every emphasis x intent x enabled state on both surfaces: glyph 6.05:1 minimum (accent error, rest), 3:1 required (WCAG 1.4.11); focus ring 11.73:1 or more against the surfaces. Light unchanged: glyph 4.75:1 minimum, focus ring 5.45:1 or more.

Initial draft. Decisions icons-material-symbols and name-from-label. Emphasis (accent, subtle, ghost), intent (neutral, brand, error), sizes (xsmall to large), states and color tokens mirror Button 0.8.0 (provisional until decided for the icon button); the container is square (min-width = min-height, 24 to 48 px; 44 pt on iOS, 48 dp on Android). Glyph contrast against the container, every emphasis x intent x enabled state on both surfaces: 4.75:1 minimum (subtle error, pressed), 3:1 required (WCAG 1.4.11). Focus ring 5.45:1 or more against the surfaces.
